17400:
To whitewash something literally means to paint a surface — usually a wall, a fence, or a building — with a thin white liquid made from lime or chalk mixed with water. This gives the surface a clean, bright white appearance. Think of the classic image of a gleaming white village wall in the countryside. That wall was whitewashed.

This physical act is the root of everything. Notice what whitewashing does: it covers the surface. Cracks, stains, dirt, rough patches — they're all hidden under that fresh white coat. The problems are still there underneath, but you can't see them anymore.

That idea — hiding what's really there by making the surface look clean — is exactly how the word works in its more powerful, more commonly used senses.
The most important meaning: Covering up wrongdoing

This is the sense you will encounter most often, and it is the heart of the word.

To whitewash means to deliberately hide, minimize, or cover up something bad — a mistake, a crime, a scandal, a failure — so that the truth does not come out and the people responsible don't face consequences. The goal is to make something corrupt or shameful look clean, acceptable, or normal.

A few things are almost always true when this word is used this way:

It is deliberate. This is never accidental. Someone is actively working to suppress the truth. The concealment is intentional.

It usually involves power. Whitewashing is typically done by governments, institutions, corporations, authorities, or officials — people and organizations that have the influence to control information and shape public perception.

The bad things still exist underneath. Just like the cracks in the wall that the paint covers, the wrongdoing hasn't gone away. It has just been hidden. This is what makes whitewashing so dishonest — it creates a false appearance of cleanliness while the rot remains.

It involves a surface-level clean-up. Often, whitewashing isn't total silence. It may involve a fake inquiry, a misleading report, a carefully worded official statement, or a biased investigation that reaches a convenient conclusion. The appearance of examining the problem is created, while the problem itself is quietly buried.

Example sentences:

  • The government whitewashed the entire scandal by appointing a committee made up of its own allies, who unsurprisingly cleared every official of wrongdoing.
  • The company whitewashed its role in the environmental disaster by funding a study that downplayed the damage it had caused.
  • The report whitewashed the police's use of excessive force, framing it as a proportional response.
Portraying someone or something in a falsely positive light

Closely related to the above, to whitewash someone or something can also mean to describe them in a way that is unrealistically favorable — leaving out their flaws, failures, or wrongdoings, and presenting only the good parts.

This is slightly different from covering up a specific scandal. Here, it's more about selective presentation over time — like a biography that praises a historical leader while completely ignoring the atrocities they committed, or a documentary that celebrates a company's rise while never mentioning the workers it exploited along the way.

Example sentences:

  • The official biography whitewashes the dictator, portraying him as a visionary while making no mention of the thousands imprisoned during his rule.
  • The history textbook whitewashes the colonial era, framing it purely as a story of progress and civilization.
In sports: A complete, shutout victory

In sports — particularly in cricket, but also used in football, tennis, and other games — to whitewash an opponent means to defeat them completely in every single match or game of a series, giving them zero wins.

The image is the same: the opponent's slate is wiped clean — they have nothing to show for the series. It's a total defeat.

Example sentences:

  • India whitewashed England 5–0 in the one-day series, winning every single match.
  • The home team whitewashed their rivals in the tournament, not dropping a single game.
In media and culture: Racial whitewashing

In modern usage, especially in discussions about film, television, and literature, whitewash has taken on a specific meaning related to race.

To whitewash a character or a story means to replace a non-white character, cultural role, or historical figure with a white person — usually through casting a white actor in a role that was originally written for, or should naturally belong to, a person of colour. It can also refer to rewriting stories from non-white cultures and traditions in ways that center white perspectives and erase the original culture.

Example sentences:

  • Critics accused the film of whitewashing the story by casting a white American actress in the role of a Japanese warrior.
  • The studio whitewashed the source material, stripping away the South Asian cultural setting and replacing it with a generic Western one.

No matter which sense is being used, whitewash always carries the same core idea: making something look clean, pure, or acceptable when it isn't. Whether it's a physical wall, a political scandal, a historical record, a person's reputation, a sports contest, or cultural representation — whitewashing is about applying a false, smooth surface over something that is far more complicated, flawed, or dark underneath.

This is also why the word almost always carries a negative connotation. You would rarely say someone "whitewashed" something and mean it as a compliment. The word implies deception, dishonesty, and a deliberate suppression of truth.

• The committee whitewashed the findings. (simple past)
  • They are whitewashing the scandal. (present continuous — an active, ongoing cover-up)
  • The report was completely whitewashed. (passive — the report had its uncomfortable truths removed)
  • This is nothing but a whitewash. (used as a noun — the entire effort is described as a cover-up)
  • The whitewashing of history is dangerous. (gerund — the act of falsely sanitizing history)

SenseCore Idea

Literal: Painting a surface white to make it look clean.

Figurative (most common): Hiding wrongdoing, scandal, or failure — especially by those in power — to protect reputations and avoid accountability.

Flattering portrayal: Describing someone or something in a way that ignores all the bad and shows only the good.

Sports: Defeating an opponent completely, leaving them with no wins.

Cultural/racial: Replacing non-white characters, stories, or identities with white ones in media.

The word is powerful precisely because it is so visual. Every time you hear it, picture that fresh white paint going over a cracked, stained, dirty wall — and you will understand exactly what is happening.
17401:
To whittle something means to shape or reduce it by making many small, repeated cuts or removals — slowly, patiently, bit by bit, until you get what you want.

Think of it this way: you are not hacking something apart all at once. You are chipping away at it in tiny pieces, over and over, until the shape or size you want emerges.

In its original, physical sense, to whittle means to carve a piece of wood into a shape by repeatedly cutting thin shavings off it with a knife.

Imagine an old craftsman sitting on a porch with a small block of wood and a knife. He doesn't make one deep cut. Instead, he makes hundreds of small, shallow slices — shaving off a little here, a little there — until the block slowly transforms into a duck, a spoon, a walking stick, or a figure.

That slow, careful, repetitive process of cutting away small bits of wood with a blade is whittling.

Examples:

  • He whittled a knife handle out of a branch he found in the forest.
  • She sat by the fire and whittled a small bird from a piece of oak.
  • The boy learned to whittle a simple peg using just a penknife.

Notice that what you start with is always larger and rougher, and what you end up with is smaller, refined, and shaped. The act of whittling removes what doesn't belong until the intended form appears.

When used literally, you typically whittle wood — sticks, branches, blocks, or pieces of timber. You can whittle something into a final shape, or whittle from a raw material:

  • He whittled the stick into a sharp point.
  • She whittled a figure from a soft piece of pine.

This is where the word becomes especially useful in everyday life. "Whittle" is very commonly used figuratively to describe gradually reducing something — a number, an amount, a list, a problem — by making small, repeated reductions over time.

Just as wood is reduced shaving by shaving until something smaller and more precise remains, anything else can be "whittled" when it shrinks step by step through repeated effort.

Examples:

  • They whittled the list of 200 job applicants down to just 5.
  • She whittled her debt down over three years by paying a little extra every month.
  • The team whittled the problem down to one key issue.
  • Years of small cutbacks had whittled the company's workforce from 500 to 80.

In every case, notice the same pattern: something starts large, and through many small removals over time, it becomes smaller and more focused.
The Phrasal Verbs: "Whittle Down" and "Whittle Away"

You will almost always see "whittle" used with one of these two small words attached to it. Each has a slightly different feel.

Whittle down — This means to reduce something from a larger quantity to a smaller, more manageable one. The idea is that you are cutting it down to size. There is usually a goal in mind — you want to arrive at a specific, smaller result.

  • The coach whittled the squad down from 30 players to 15.
  • Let's whittle down our options before the meeting.
  • He whittled the 10-page report down to a 2-page summary.

The focus here is on arriving at something leaner and more precise.

Whittle away — This means to reduce something slowly and continuously, often until very little (or nothing) is left. It often carries a slightly negative or regrettable tone — something is being eroded or eaten up over time, sometimes without you fully noticing.

  • Years of inflation had whittled away at their savings.
  • The endless delays whittled away at her patience.
  • Corruption whittled away at public trust over decades.

The focus here is on gradual erosion or loss, and the end result is often something depleted or diminished.
The Key Feeling of the Word

What makes "whittle" special as a word is its strong sense of gradualness and repetition. It is never about one dramatic action. It always suggests:

  • Many small steps, not one big one.
  • Time and patience are involved.
  • Something is being removed or reduced, not added to.
  • The process is deliberate, not accidental.

If someone says "we need to whittle this down," they are signalling that the work will happen in stages, through careful, repeated effort — not all at once.

To sharpen your understanding, here is what whittling is not:

  • It is not a sudden or dramatic removal. You do not whittle something in one stroke. If someone slashes a budget in one big cut, that is not whittling — it is something more abrupt.
  • It is not about adding or building up. Whittling only ever means taking away.
  • It is not random or careless. Whittling is precise and intentional, even when slow.

LiteralTo carve wood into a shape by making many small cuts with a knife
FigurativeTo gradually reduce something (a number, list, amount) through repeated small reductions
Whittle downTo reduce something to a smaller, more focused version
Whittle awayTo slowly erode or deplete something over time
Core feelingSlow, patient, repeated, deliberate reduction
One Sentence to Remember It By

To whittle is to reduce something carefully and gradually — one small cut at a time — until only what you truly need remains.

Whether it is a block of wood becoming a carving, or a list of 100 candidates becoming 3 finalists, the spirit of the word is always the same: patient, small, repeated reduction toward something better.
17402:
To whittle means to carve a piece of wood by repeatedly shaving off thin slices with a knife. Imagine a craftsman sitting on a porch, holding a rough block of wood and a sharp knife. He doesn't hack off large chunks. Instead, he makes many small, careful cuts — shaving away a little bit here, a little bit there — until the block slowly becomes a smooth, neat figure.

That image is the heart of this phrase.

When you say you are whittling something down, you mean you are gradually reducing it in size, number, or amount by removing parts of it little by little, step by step.

The key word is gradually. Whittling down is never a single, dramatic cut. It is a slow, steady process of removing pieces until you reach a smaller, more manageable result.

Think of it this way: if you have 100 job applications on your desk and you need to choose 3 candidates, you don't pick 3 immediately. You first remove the weakest applications, then review what's left, remove more, review again — and you keep going until only 3 remain. That entire process is "whittling down."

The word whittle comes from an Old English word thwitel, which simply meant a large knife used for cutting. By the 1500s, "to whittle" became a verb meaning to carve wood with a knife. Over time, people noticed how well the image described any process of slow reduction, and the figurative meaning was born.

The word "down" was added to emphasize the direction of the change — things are going down in size or number.
The Exact Nuance You Must Understand

This phrase carries two very specific feelings that you should never forget:

1. It is gradual, not sudden.
You do not whittle down something in one move. It happens over multiple steps or over a period of time. This is what separates "whittle down" from a word like "cut," which can be immediate.

2. It moves toward a smaller, cleaner result.
The woodcarver is not just making random cuts. He has a target shape in mind. Similarly, when you whittle down a list, a budget, or a group, you are working toward a specific, smaller goal. There is a purpose and a direction.
How It Is Used in Grammar

"Whittle down" is a phrasal verb, which means it is a verb + a small word ("down") that together form a single meaning.

It is a transitive phrasal verb, which means it always needs an object — something being whittled down. You cannot just say "we whittled down." You must say "we whittled down the list" or "we whittled down our expenses."

Here are the most common sentence patterns:

Pattern 1: Whittle down + object
"We need to whittle down our expenses."

Pattern 2: Whittle down + object + to + final number/size
"She whittled the list down to five names."
"They whittled their debt down to almost nothing."

Pattern 3: Whittle down + object + from + starting point + to + end point
"The company whittled the number of applicants down from 200 to 10."

Pattern 4: Whittle down + object + by + amount
"They whittled down the budget by 30 percent."

Notice that "down" can move around a little. You can say "whittle down the list" or "whittle the list down" — both are correct.

Here are examples across different areas of life, so you can see how naturally this phrase applies everywhere:

In a job search:
"The hiring team had 500 applications. After the first round, they whittled the pool down to 50. After interviews, they whittled it down further to just 8 finalists."

In finance:
"He started with $20,000 in credit card debt. Over three years, he whittled it down to zero by making extra payments every month."

In planning:
"We had fifteen ideas for the project, but we sat together and whittled them down to the three most practical ones."

In a competition:
"Sixty teams entered the tournament. Round by round, the number was whittled down until only two remained for the final."

In writing:
"Her first draft was 10,000 words. Her editor helped her whittle it down to a tight, punchy 4,000 words."

In daily life:
"I had a to-do list of twenty things. By evening, I had whittled it down to four."

Almost anything that exists in a quantity or size that you want to reduce. Common examples include:

  • A list (of names, options, tasks, candidates)
  • A number (of applicants, contestants, items)
  • A budget or cost
  • Debt
  • Time remaining on something
  • A lead in a competition (the gap between two scores can be whittled down)
  • A document or piece of writing (its word count, its length)
  • Choices or options
Related Phrases and How They Differ

Understanding "whittle down" more deeply means knowing how it compares to similar phrases.

Whittle away (at something) — This is slightly different. "Whittle away" focuses on the erosion itself, often without a clear endpoint in mind. It can sometimes carry a negative feeling of something being slowly eaten up.
"Years of worry had whittled away at his confidence." — Here, confidence is being eroded gradually, not purposefully reduced toward a goal.

Narrow down — This also means to reduce a set of options, but it focuses more on focusing and zeroing in on the right answer. "Narrow down" is used mostly for choices and possibilities.
"We've narrowed down the cause of the error to two possibilities."

Pare down — Very similar to "whittle down." "Pare" literally means to peel the skin of a fruit with a knife. "Pare down" is slightly more formal and often used for costs, expenses, and written content.
"We need to pare down the report to the essential points."

Cut down — Also similar, but this can happen in one step and lacks the feeling of gradualness. "Cut down" feels more abrupt.
"They cut down the workforce by 200 people." — This sounds like it happened in one announcement.

Reduce — A general, neutral word for making something smaller. It has no special flavor of gradualness or process. "Whittle down" is more vivid and specific.

"Whittle down" sits comfortably in the middle of the formality scale. It is not slang, so you can use it in professional writing, business meetings, and serious conversations. But it is also not stiff or overly formal, so it works perfectly in casual speech and everyday writing.

You will see it in newspaper articles, business reports, sports commentary, casual emails, and everyday conversation equally comfortably. It is a versatile, well-respected phrase in English.
The One-Line Summary to Lock It In Memory

Imagine that carver slowly cutting a block of wood into a clean shape — that slow, deliberate, step-by-step reduction is exactly what you do when you whittle something down: you reduce it gradually, in stages, until it reaches the smaller size, number, or amount you want.
17403:
A whodunit is a story — a novel, film, play, or TV show — whose central puzzle is a mystery crime (almost always a murder), and whose entire plot is built around the question: who committed it?

The audience doesn't know who the criminal is. Neither do most of the characters. The story's engine is the gradual uncovering of that answer.

A whodunit has a few essential ingredients:

A crime, usually murder. The story almost always opens with a body. Someone has been killed, and the circumstances are deliberately obscure. The how and when matter, but the driving question is always the who.

Suspects. There are multiple characters who could have done it. Each has a possible motive (a reason to want the victim dead), an opportunity (they were in the right place at the right time), or both. The skill of the author is in making several suspects seem equally plausible — keeping you genuinely uncertain.

Clues and red herrings. The story scatters clues — small details, strange behaviours, inconsistencies — that point toward the truth. But it also scatters red herrings: false clues deliberately designed to mislead you into suspecting the wrong person. A good whodunit is a fair game: all the information needed to solve it is given to you, but disguised well enough that most readers miss it.

A detective figure. There is usually a central character — a detective, an amateur sleuth, a sharp-minded outsider — who gathers evidence, questions suspects, and eventually works out the answer. This character is your guide through the puzzle.

A revelation. The whodunit climaxes with an unmasking. The detective (or story) reveals who did it, why, and how — and all the scattered clues suddenly snap into a clear, logical picture. This moment of revelation is one of the most satisfying experiences the genre offers.

A whodunit is fundamentally a puzzle dressed up as a story. The author and the reader are in a quiet contest: the author hides the truth cleverly; you try to find it before it's revealed. This is why fans of the genre often read with their minds actively working — noticing things, forming theories, reconsidering them.

Crucially, a whodunit operates by rules. The guilty party must be someone who actually appeared in the story — not a stranger introduced at the last page. The solution must be logically consistent with every clue given. The reader must have, in theory, a fair chance of solving it. This sense of fair play is what separates a satisfying whodunit from a cheap trick.

Whodunits are not a single mood. They exist across a wide range:

  • Cosy whodunits are light, charming, and relatively gentle. The murder happens "off-screen," the village setting is quaint, and the detective is often an ordinary person — a librarian, a retired teacher, a nosy neighbour — rather than a hard-boiled professional. Death is treated more as an intellectual puzzle than a visceral horror.
  • Classic or "golden age" whodunits are the refined, puzzle-centred mysteries from the early-to-mid 20th century — elegant plots, country houses, dinner parties, and a detective who is more brain than brawn.
  • Darker whodunits blend the puzzle with psychological depth, social commentary, or genuine menace. The mystery is still central, but the tone is heavier and more unsettling.

Despite these variations, the defining feature remains constant: you don't know who did it until the story tells you.

The word is inseparable from certain names:

Agatha Christie is the undisputed queen of the whodunit. Her novels — featuring detectives like Hercule Poirot and Miss Marple — are the gold standard of the form. And Then There Were None, Murder on the Orient Express, and The Murder of Roger Ackroyd are among the most celebrated whodunits ever written.

Arthur Conan Doyle's Sherlock Holmes stories are close cousins — though Holmes stories lean more toward how and why than purely who, they share the same DNA.

In film and television: Knives Out (2019) and its sequels are modern, self-aware whodunits. Clue (1985) is a beloved comedic take. The TV series Columbo, Poirot, and Agatha Christie's Miss Marple have made the genre a staple of television drama.

Even the board game Cluedo (Clue) — where players deduce which character committed murder, in which room, with which weapon — is a whodunit reduced to its purest mechanical form.

"Whodunit" is used both literally and loosely in everyday language.

Literally, it names the genre:

  • "She loves whodunits — she's read every Agatha Christie novel twice."
  • "The film is a classic whodunit set in a snowbound hotel."

Loosely, people borrow the word to describe any real-life situation where the identity of a wrongdoer is unknown and being investigated — with a slightly playful or ironic tone:

  • "The office fridge kept getting raided. It became a real whodunit."
  • "Investigators called the data breach the biggest corporate whodunit of the decade."

In this looser usage, the word carries a hint of wit — it treats a real mystery as though it were a story, with suspects and clues waiting to be unravelled.

A whodunit is not the same as every mystery story, even though the terms are sometimes muddled.

  • A thriller centres on danger and suspense — you know who the villain is, and the tension is whether the hero can stop them in time. A whodunit conceals the villain's identity; a thriller usually does not.
  • A heist story might involve crime, but the focus is on how a crime is pulled off, not on discovering who did it.
  • A procedural (like many police dramas) follows investigators step by step, but the audience often knows the criminal from the start — the story is about the process of catching them, not the puzzle of identifying them.

The whodunit's uniqueness lies precisely in that withheld identity — the story is about the not-knowing, and the pleasure is in the finding-out.

A whodunit is a mystery story built entirely around one question: who committed the crime? It gives you suspects, clues, and misdirection, and asks you to figure it out before the reveal. It is a genre defined by fair-play puzzlement, the pleasure of deduction, and the satisfaction of an answer that, in hindsight, makes perfect sense.
17404: The word wholesale has two distinct meanings depending on context — one rooted in commerce, the other used more broadly in everyday language. Both share the same underlying idea: large scale, all at once, not piece by piece.

In business and trade, wholesale describes the buying and selling of goods in large quantities, usually from a manufacturer or supplier to a retailer or another business — not directly to the end customer.

Think of it this way: a factory produces 10,000 bottles of shampoo. A wholesaler buys all of them at once at a very low price per bottle (because of the sheer volume). That wholesaler then sells batches of, say, 500 bottles to various shop owners. Those shop owners (retailers) then sell individual bottles to you, the customer, at a much higher price.

So anything described as wholesale in a business context is tied to this bulk, business-to-business transaction:

  • A wholesale price is the low price charged when goods are sold in bulk — far cheaper than what you'd pay in a shop.
  • A wholesale market is a place where traders buy and sell goods in large quantities.
  • A wholesale supplier is a company that sells goods in bulk to businesses, not to individual shoppers.
  • A wholesale deal is a transaction involving a large volume of goods.

The crucial point is that wholesale sits between the manufacturer and the retailer. It is not the final step of selling to the public — that's retail.

This contrast is worth understanding clearly, because the two words define each other.

WholesaleBulk, large quantities, sold to businesses, low per-unit price
RetailSmall quantities, sold to individual consumers, higher per-unit price

When a shop owner buys 200 jackets from a supplier, that's a wholesale transaction. When you walk into that shop and buy one jacket, that's retail. The same jacket has a wholesale price and a retail price — and the retail price is always higher, because the retailer needs to cover costs and make a profit on top of what they paid wholesale.

Outside of business, wholesale is used as an adjective to mean sweeping, on a large scale, total, or indiscriminate — affecting many things or people all at once, without exception or selectivity.

This meaning captures the same spirit as the commercial one: just as wholesale buying means taking everything in bulk rather than picking items one by one, wholesale used figuratively means something done in one massive sweep, not carefully, not partially.

Examples:

  • "The new government announced wholesale changes to the tax system."
    → Not small tweaks here and there, but a complete, sweeping overhaul of the entire system.
  • "The flood caused wholesale destruction of the village."
    → The destruction was total and indiscriminate — everything was wiped out, not just isolated parts.
  • "There was a wholesale rejection of the proposal by the committee."
    → Every single part of it was rejected; nothing was accepted. A complete, blanket rejection.
  • "The company underwent wholesale restructuring."
    → The restructuring was massive and comprehensive — affecting the entire organization, not just one department.

You can feel the difference when you compare it to a more limited alternative:

  • "The company made a few small changes." (selective, limited)
  • "The company made wholesale changes." (sweeping, total, large-scale)

The figurative use often carries a slight tone of drama or seriousness — it implies the scale is significant and the impact is broad.
The Thread That Connects Both Meanings

Both meanings of wholesale share a common thread: bulk, totality, and scale. Whether you're talking about buying 10,000 units of a product at once, or describing a change that overhauls an entire system from top to bottom — the word always signals that something is happening in a big, all-encompassing way, not in small, careful, individual pieces.

If you remember just one idea about this word, let it be this: wholesale = large-scale, all at once, not piecemeal.
Common Collocations (Words You'll Often See With "Wholesale")

• Wholesale price / wholesale cost — the bulk price
  • Wholesale market / wholesale trade — trading in bulk
  • Wholesale changes / wholesale reform — sweeping, total changes
  • Wholesale destruction / wholesale slaughter — total, indiscriminate destruction
  • Wholesale adoption — adopting something fully and completely
  • Wholesale rejection / wholesale dismissal — complete rejection without exception

ContextWhat "wholesale" means
Business / CommerceRelated to buying/selling in bulk, between businesses, at low per-unit prices
General / FigurativeSweeping, large-scale, total, indiscriminate — affecting everything at once

Both senses are common, so you'll encounter this word in financial news ("wholesale inflation"), in politics ("wholesale policy reforms"), in descriptions of damage or change ("wholesale destruction"), and in everyday business talk ("wholesale prices"). Recognizing the context will always tell you which meaning is in play.
17405:
Wholesome means genuinely and completely good — good in a way that nourishes you, benefits you, and leaves nothing harmful hiding underneath.

Think of it this way: the word carries the idea that something is good all the way through, not just on the surface. Pure, real, and beneficial. No hidden rot.
The Four Main Ways It's Used

1. Wholesome food

When food is called wholesome, it means it's natural, nutritious, and genuinely good for your body. Simple, real ingredients. Nothing artificial or processed.

"She grew up eating wholesome meals — rice, vegetables, lentils, cooked fresh every day."

Compare this to just saying "healthy." "Healthy" focuses mainly on nutrition. "Wholesome" adds a sense of simplicity, naturalness, and genuine nourishment. A wholesome meal feels real — like something a grandmother would cook, not something from a factory.

2. Wholesome values, content, or entertainment

When a movie, book, story, or show is called wholesome, it means the content promotes good values — kindness, honesty, family, friendship — and contains nothing disturbing, violent, sexual, or morally harmful. It's safe and uplifting for anyone, including children.

"It was a wholesome film — no violence, no dark themes. Just a story about a boy and his dog."

"They wanted wholesome entertainment for their family movie night."

This doesn't mean it has to be boring or childish. It simply means the content leaves you feeling uplifted, not disturbed.

3. A wholesome person

When you describe a person as wholesome, you mean they have genuine, sincere goodness in their character. They're kind, honest, decent, and morally upright — not because they're performing it for others, but because that's truly who they are. There's no meanness, pettiness, or hidden agenda in them.

"He's the most wholesome person I know — he never gossips, never puts people down, and always shows up when you need him."

A wholesome person radiates authentic warmth. The key word here is genuine — their goodness is real, not an act.

4. A wholesome moment or interaction

This is probably the most common use in modern everyday language and especially on the internet. A wholesome moment is one that is genuinely heartwarming — a small act of kindness, a sincere gesture, something that makes you feel that the world isn't so bad after all.

"A little girl gave her umbrella to a stray dog sitting in the rain. It was the most wholesome thing I've seen all week."

"That wholesome moment when your grandpa learns to video call just to say goodnight."

Online, "wholesome memes" are a whole genre — content designed not to make you laugh cruelly at someone, but to make you smile, feel warm, and feel good about humanity.

"Wholesome" carries a very specific emotional warmth. When you call something wholesome, you're not just saying it's good — you're saying it's purely, sincerely, and gently good. It has a soft, comforting quality to it.

It's the feeling of:

  • A child helping an elderly person cross the road
  • A family cooking together on a Sunday
  • A friend checking in on you just because
  • Simple food made with care
  • A story that ends with everyone being kind to each other

The word feels the opposite of cynical, cruel, corrupt, or artificial.
How It Differs from Similar Words

ConceptWhat It Focuses On
  • Healthy is mainly about the body. "Wholesome" covers the body, the mind, and moral character all at once.
  • Innocent means free from wrongdoing or naivety. "Wholesome" means actively good, not just free from bad.
  • Pure focuses on the absence of contamination. "Wholesome" emphasizes the presence of genuine goodness.
  • Decent means meeting a basic moral standard. "Wholesome" is warmer and richer than that — it has heart.

• It doesn't mean perfect. A wholesome person can make mistakes; they're just genuinely good at their core.
  • It doesn't mean naïve or simple-minded. You can be wise, experienced, and still wholesome.
  • It doesn't mean boring. Some people use "too wholesome" slightly teasingly when something is almost unbelievably nice, but that's not the word's real meaning.
  • It doesn't mean religious, though it's often associated with traditional values.
A Few More Examples Across Contexts

"He had a wholesome childhood — open fields, family dinners, no worries."

"The bakery sold wholesome bread — just flour, water, salt, and time."

"Their friendship is so wholesome. They've known each other since kindergarten and still write letters."

"I needed something wholesome after all those dark crime shows, so I watched a baking competition."

"That video of the soldier reuniting with his dog is pure wholesome content."

Wholesome = genuinely and completely good — in a way that nourishes you, uplifts you, and has nothing harmful or false hiding inside it.

If something is wholesome, it's the real thing. Real goodness. Real warmth. Real benefit.
17406: "Wholly" means completely and entirely — 100%, with absolutely nothing left out, left over, or held back. When you use "wholly," you are saying that something applies in full, with zero exceptions.
What it does in a sentence

"Wholly" is an adverb, so it modifies (describes or strengthens) other words — usually adjectives, verbs, or past participles.

  • It can sit before an adjective:
    "The plan was wholly unnecessary." → The plan was unnecessary in every single way, not even a little bit necessary.
  • It can sit before a verb:
    "I wholly disagree." → My disagreement is total. There is no part of me that agrees.
  • It can sit before a past participle (a verb used as a description):
    "She was wholly devoted to her work." → Every bit of her devotion went toward her work. None of it was divided or partial.
The key idea: "no part left out"

Think of a pie. If something is "wholly" true, the entire pie is truth — not 80%, not 99%, but the full, uncut pie. There is no slice missing.

This is what makes "wholly" powerful and precise. It shuts the door on any grey area. Consider:

  • "He is wholly responsible for the mistake." → The responsibility lands entirely on him. No one else shares it. Not even a little.
  • "The theory is wholly wrong." → The theory fails in every part, not just some parts.

One of the most frequent and useful ways "wholly" appears is in the phrase "not wholly", which is a polite and precise way of saying "not completely" or "only partly."

  • "I am not wholly convinced by his argument." → I see some merit in it, but I'm not fully persuaded. Part of me still doubts.
  • "The situation is not wholly bad." → Some parts of it are actually okay.

This construction is very common in careful, thoughtful writing when you want to avoid being absolute.

"Wholly" means essentially the same thing as entirely, completely, fully, and totally — but with some practical differences:

Wholly leans formal and precise. You'll see it more in written English, legal documents, academic papers, formal essays, and journalism — less often in casual speech.

Totally and completely are more conversational and everyday:

  • Casual: "I totally agree."
  • Formal: "I wholly agree."

Entirely is the closest sibling to "wholly" and they can usually swap places without changing meaning. "Wholly" is just slightly more elevated in tone.

Fully often refers to reaching a complete state or potential, like "fully prepared" or "fully grown", whereas "wholly" is more about exclusivity and totality of a quality.

"Wholly" sometimes carries the extra shade of meaning "and nothing else" — suggesting the thing belongs entirely to one cause, one person, or one quality, without being shared or divided.

  • "The credit is wholly yours." → You alone deserve it. No one else gets a share.
  • "This is a wholly personal decision." → It's purely personal; it has nothing to do with anyone else or any other factor.

You will often see "wholly owned" in business and legal language:

"Company A is a wholly owned subsidiary of Company B."

This means Company B owns 100% of Company A — not 60%, not 90%, but every single share. The word "wholly" here does critical legal work: it rules out any partial ownership.

Use "wholly" when you want to:

  • State something is absolutely and completely the case, with no exceptions
  • Stress that something is undivided — not partial, not mixed
  • Sound precise and formal rather than casual
  • Use the phrase "not wholly" to signal a nuanced, partial disagreement or uncertainty

Avoid using it in casual speech where "totally" or "completely" would sound more natural. But in writing, formal discussions, or arguments where precision matters, "wholly" is a sharp and reliable tool.
A few more examples to cement it

SentenceWhat it really means
"She was not wholly wrong."She had some valid points, even if the overall position was flawed.
"The building was wholly destroyed."Nothing was left standing. Total destruction.
"His success is wholly due to hard work."Hard work — and only that — explains his success. Luck, connections, privilege? None of that.
"I don't wholly understand this yet."I understand some of it, but not all of it.
"The decision was wholly ours."No outside force made it for us. It belonged entirely to us.

In one line: "Wholly" = 100%, completely, in every part, with no share left out — and it says so with quiet formality and precision.
17407:
To whoop means to make a loud, sharp, enthusiastic cry or shout. It is the sound a person makes when they are suddenly overcome with a strong emotion — most often joy, excitement, or triumph. It is not a calm, quiet expression. It is an explosion of feeling that bursts out of you before you even think about it.

Think of a child on Christmas morning who runs downstairs, sees the presents, and yells out loud. That cry — that instinctive, explosive shout of joy — is a whoop.

What makes "whoop" special is that it captures a very specific type of shout. It is not:

  • the scream of fear
  • the cry of pain
  • the groan of disappointment

It is almost always positive and energetic. It suggests release — like pressure that has been building finally shoots out in one loud burst.

Examples:

  • "The crowd whooped when the home team scored."
  • "She whooped with delight when she heard she got the job."
  • "He whooped and punched the air after finishing the race."

You can also whoop at or for someone to urge them on, cheer them up, or celebrate them. In this sense, you are directing your enthusiastic cry toward another person.

Examples:

  • "The audience whooped and cheered for the performer."
  • "His friends whooped for him as he crossed the finish line."

This is the kind of whooping you hear at concerts, sports events, and celebrations — it is a crowd's way of saying "Yes! We love this! More!"

In informal, everyday American English, "whoop" also means to defeat someone decisively and convincingly — to beat them badly in a game, contest, or fight.

Examples:

  • "Our team whooped them 9–1."
  • "She whooped her opponent in just three rounds."
  • "I whooped him at chess every single time we played."

Here, the connection to the original meaning still exists beneath the surface — when you defeat someone so thoroughly, you feel like whooping (shouting) with joy. Over time, the act of defeating someone came to be called "whooping" them.

"Whoop it up" is a common informal phrase meaning to celebrate loudly and enthusiastically, or to have a wild, lively, noisy good time.

Examples:

  • "After the championship win, the whole city was whooping it up."
  • "They whooped it up all night at the graduation party."

It paints a picture of people being unrestrained in their happiness — shouting, laughing, dancing, letting loose.
The Medical Sense (Specific but Worth Knowing)

In a more specific, medical context, "whoop" describes the sharp, gasping, high-pitched sound a person makes when they breathe in during a severe coughing fit — particularly in the illness called whooping cough. The patient coughs violently and then inhales with a loud "whoop" sound as they struggle for air.

Example:

  • "The child coughed repeatedly and then whooped as he gasped for breath."

This usage is narrower and you will mostly encounter it in medical or historical descriptions, not in everyday conversation.

All these meanings share one common thread: a loud, sharp, forceful outburst. Whether it is joy, encouragement, triumph over an opponent, wild celebration, or a gasping breath — "whooping" always involves something intense and unrestrained breaking through. It is never subtle. It is never quiet. It is always vivid, alive, and impossible to ignore.
17408:
Whopping means extremely large — larger than what you'd normally expect, larger than what seems ordinary, and large enough to make someone stop and notice.

It doesn't just describe something big. It describes something remarkably, strikingly, almost unbelievably big.

Think of it this way: "big" is a neutral description. "Whopping" is big with shock or emphasis baked into it.
What kinds of "big" does it describe?

This is important: whopping doesn't only describe physical size. It describes largeness in a very broad sense:

  • A large number → "a whopping 50,000 people showed up"
  • A large amount of money → "a whopping ₹5 crore fine"
  • A large quantity → "a whopping pile of work"
  • A large degree or extent → "a whopping increase in prices"
  • A large mistake or lie → "a whopping blunder" / "a whopping lie"

So whenever something is far greater in size, number, amount, or degree than what seems normal or expected — that's the territory of "whopping."

Here's what separates "whopping" from plain words like "large," "great," or "huge":

Whopping carries a tone of surprise, disbelief, or strong emphasis. It signals: "Look at how extraordinarily large this is — don't just pass over it, notice it!"

When someone says, "She won a whopping ₹2 crore on a game show," the word "whopping" is doing two jobs at once:

  1. Telling you the amount is very large.
  2. Telling you that the speaker finds this amount staggering, remarkable, worth highlighting.

It's the difference between:

  • "He ate five burgers." ← a plain fact
  • "He ate a whopping five burgers." ← five burgers?! That's astonishing!
Where it sits in a sentence

As an adjective, "whopping" almost always appears directly before the noun or number it describes. This is called an attributive position.

You say:

"a whopping sum of money" ✅
"a whopping 300 employees" ✅
"a whopping error" ✅

You would not normally say:

"The sum was whopping." ❌ ← This sounds unnatural.

The word needs to sit right in front of what it's modifying — it doesn't stand alone well as a predicate adjective.
Register: where and when it's used

"Whopping" is an informal word. It lives comfortably in:

  • Everyday conversation
  • Casual writing
  • Journalism and news headlines (very common there — "Firm pays whopping ₹100 crore in penalties")
  • Blog posts, social media

It does not belong in:

  • Formal essays or academic writing
  • Official reports or legal documents
  • Business proposals

If you're writing something formal, you'd replace it with "enormous," "substantial," "massive," or "considerable."
Is it positive, negative, or neutral?

The word itself is neutral — it doesn't judge whether the big thing is good or bad. What makes it feel positive or negative is the context:

  • "A whopping bonus" → feels exciting, positive
  • "A whopping tax bill" → feels painful, negative
  • "A whopping crowd turned out for the protest" → neutral, just emphatic

In every case, the word only says: this is larger than you'd think. The context decides if that's good news or bad news.

There's one interesting non-size usage worth knowing. When people say "a whopping lie" or "a whopping exaggeration," they aren't talking about a physically big lie — they mean an outrageous, audacious, extreme lie. Here, "whopping" extends from "big in size" to "big in degree of outrageousness."

This is the same root idea (= extremely, remarkably great), just applied to the scale of the dishonesty rather than a physical or numerical quantity.

Whenever you're deciding whether to use "whopping," ask yourself: Is this so large that it deserves to be highlighted or would surprise people? If yes, "whopping" fits. If the size is ordinary or just slightly above average, it's an overstatement.

You wouldn't say "a whopping 3% increase" unless 3% is genuinely surprising in that specific context. But "a whopping 300% increase"? Absolutely.
Whopping is an informal adjective meaning extremely and surprisingly large — in size, number, amount, or degree — used when you want to emphasize that something is far beyond the ordinary.
17409:
A whorl is anything that forms a circular, spiraling, or swirling arrangement around a central point — like a coil, a curl, or a ring that winds around itself or a center.

Think of water going down a drain. It doesn't just fall straight down — it spins in a circular pattern as it drains. That spinning, spiraling shape is the essence of a whorl. Or think of a snail's shell: it winds around and around a central axis in ever-growing loops. Each complete loop of that shell is a whorl.

The key idea is always circular or spiral movement locked into a structure or pattern. Whorls can be flat and ring-like, or they can coil through space like a spring.

1. Fingerprints

This is probably the most common modern use. Fingerprint experts classify all fingerprints into three basic types: arches, loops, and whorls. A whorl fingerprint is one where the ridges of your skin form a complete circular or oval spiral around a central point — like a tiny whirlpool on the tip of your finger. If you look at your own fingertips under good light and see that the lines seem to swirl around a center without exiting either side, you have a whorl. Roughly a third of all fingerprints are whorls.

2. Shells (Snails, Nautilus, Conch)

When a snail's shell spirals outward from its tip to its opening, each full 360-degree revolution of that spiral is called one whorl. A shell with many tight coils has many whorls. A flat, open spiral shell might have just a few wide ones. The word captures both the shape and the act of winding: the shell is built up whorl by whorl as the snail grows.

3. Hair

You know the swirling patch of hair on the back of someone's head, or the spiral at the crown where the hair seems to radiate outward from a single point? That's a whorl — also commonly called a cowlick when it's at the front. Dogs, cats, horses, and many other animals have them too, and animal breeders sometimes pay close attention to where on the body these hair whorls appear.

4. Plants (Botany)

In plants, a whorl describes leaves, petals, or other parts that are arranged in a ring around the stem — all at the same height, radiating outward like the spokes of a wheel. For example, if a plant has three leaves growing at the same point on the stem, spread equally around it (rather than alternating or growing in pairs), those three leaves form a whorl. Many flowers are described as having whorls of petals, whorls of sepals, and whorls of stamens — each ring of parts is its own whorl. This is actually how flowers are described scientifically: as a series of concentric whorls, one inside the other.

5. Shells of Ears

The outer ear (the visible, fleshy part on the side of your head) has a folded, ridged structure. The curved ridges and folds of the outer ear are sometimes described as whorls, since they spiral and curl around each other. Anatomically, the inner coiled structure of the ear (the cochlea) is also described in terms of whorls — it completes roughly two and a half turns, and each turn is a whorl.

6. Wood Grain

When you look at a cross-section of a tree trunk or a wooden plank, you sometimes see a circular pattern in the grain — especially around the spot where a branch once grew. This circular, swirling pattern in the wood is a whorl. Woodworkers and carpenters encounter this regularly, and a whorl in the wood can affect how the piece behaves when cut or shaped.

7. General / Literary Use

Writers and poets use "whorl" to describe anything with a beautiful, circular, or spiraling quality — the swirling pattern in a pool of water, the curling shape of smoke, the spiral of a galaxy, the coiling of a rope. It's a word that evokes elegance and natural symmetry.
What Makes Something a Whorl vs. Just a Curve?

A simple curve bends but doesn't close into a circle or spiral. A whorl specifically involves the sense of going around — either completing a circle, spiraling inward or outward, or coiling through space. The motion implied is rotational: something has wound, curled, or swirled around a point.

A single gentle S-curve in a river is not a whorl. But if that river were to spiral into a tight whirlpool — that's a whorl. The difference is circularity and rotation.

Think of the word whirl — as in, something spinning fast. Whorl is the same root idea, but as a noun for the result of that spinning: the shape left behind when something has whirled. A whorl is a whirl, frozen in form.
A whorl is a circular or spiral arrangement — whether of fingerprint ridges, shell coils, hair, plant parts, or wood grain — where something winds or radiates around a central point.
